clinicalPearls: Chemical burns result from corrosive substances contacting skin, eyes or mucous membranes, commonly in industrial, cleaning and laboratory settings
Immediate and copious irrigation with water for a prolonged period is the priority first aid for most chemical skin and eye exposures, and should not be delayed while identifying the agent

Alkalis typically cause deeper, progressive liquefactive injury that penetrates over time, whereas acids tend to produce coagulative injury with a more defined eschar; hydrofluoric acid is a special case
Hydrofluoric acid causes deep tissue penetration and dangerous systemic effects including hypocalcaemia and cardiac dysrhythmia, and is treated specifically with calcium
The apparent surface appearance can underestimate the true depth, which may only declare itself over hours to days
Eye exposure is a sight-threatening emergency requiring immediate, prolonged irrigation and urgent ophthalmology assessment, with pH checking to guide adequacy of rinsing
Some agents (for example phenol, hydrofluoric acid and cyanide-releasing compounds) are absorbed and cause systemic toxicity, so treat the whole patient, not just the wound
Rescuer safety, removal of contaminated clothing and correct decontamination are essential to prevent further and secondary injury
reference.pathophysiology: Corrosive chemicals damage tissue by disrupting cell membranes and denaturing or dissolving proteins and lipids. Acids cause coagulative necrosis that tends to limit their own penetration, whereas alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis that allows continued deep spread. Some agents also produce heat or are absorbed to cause systemic metabolic disturbance, such as the calcium and magnesium binding and consequent hypocalcaemia seen with hydrofluoric acid.
additionalDifferentials: Toxic epidermal necrolysis and other blistering conditions
additionalInvestigations: Identification of the chemical agent and consultation of safety data sheets or a poisons service
pH testing of the affected surface, particularly the eye, to confirm adequate irrigation
Serum calcium, magnesium, potassium and ECG monitoring after hydrofluoric acid exposure
Assessment of burn depth and surface area
Screening for systemic toxicity with agents known to be absorbed
redFlags: MEDICAL EMERGENCY: extensive or deep burns, airway or inhalational involvement, or eye exposure threatening sight
Hydrofluoric acid exposure with hypocalcaemia and cardiac dysrhythmia
Signs of systemic toxicity from absorbed agents such as phenol
Circumferential burns risking compartment syndrome or airway compromise
reference.prognosis: Prompt, thorough irrigation and appropriate specific treatment greatly improve outcome; however, deep or extensive burns, delayed decontamination, ocular involvement and systemic toxicity from certain agents can cause scarring, visual loss or death.
pitfalls: Delaying irrigation while trying to identify the chemical or find a specific antidote
Underestimating burn depth from the initial surface appearance, especially with alkalis
Failing to recognise and specifically treat hydrofluoric acid injury and its hypocalcaemia
Neglecting systemic absorption and toxicity while focusing only on the wound
Inadequate rescuer protection and decontamination leading to secondary injury
management: Immediate and copious irrigation with water for a prolonged period, begun without waiting to identify the agent, together with removal of contaminated clothing and jewellery
Identify the agent through safety data sheets or a poisons service and give agent-specific antidotes, notably topical, local or intravenous calcium for hydrofluoric acid injury
Analgesia and standard burn wound care with cleaning, appropriate dressings and tetanus prophylaxis
Monitor for systemic toxicity from absorbed agents, including electrolytes and continuous ECG after hydrofluoric acid exposure for hypocalcaemia and dysrhythmia
Reassess burn depth and area over hours to days, since surface appearance underestimates injury, with fluid resuscitation for extensive burns
Immediate prolonged irrigation and urgent ophthalmology referral for any eye involvement, guided by surface pH
Referral to a specialist burns unit for deep or extensive injury, with surgical debridement and grafting as required
Occupational health review and preventive measures to avoid recurrence
